prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "Alphabet Inc." (ticker GOOGL). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: Alphabet shows many Rule Breaker traits: top dog in search and a leader in AI and cloud, a lasting advantage from data and distribution, strong management and founders, and strong momentum (up 49.6% over 52 weeks versus 17.3% for the S&P 500). It is now a mature giant, so the 'emerging industry' trait applies mainly to Gemini, Cloud and Waymo rather than the whole company.
summaries.buffett: Alphabet has a wide moat, consistent growth and a strong net cash balance, and its retained earnings have built huge value, which fits Buffett's tenets. Against that, it has dual-class shares that limit owner influence, heavy AI capex that has cut trailing free cash flow to $53.3B, and a forward P/E of about 26 that offers no obvious margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would value Alphabet's network effects in search and YouTube, its engineering culture and its balance sheet. Inverting points to the clearest ways it could fail: AI chatbots eroding search, antitrust remedies ending default deals, and overinvestment in AI capex.
summaries.lynch: Alphabet is a fast-growing stalwart with a clear story (search ads, YouTube, Cloud and AI). Its trailing P/E of 17.8 is flattered by a $99B investment gain; on forward earnings it trades near 26 times with a PEG around 1.9, and it is far from overlooked.
summaries.fisher: Alphabet fits Fisher's points on R&D (the Transformer, TPUs, Gemini, AlphaFold), new product development (Cloud, Waymo) and margins. Fisher might mark it down for long periods of weak commercialisation of research and for founder-controlled governance that limits outside shareholders.
summaries.graham: Alphabet passes Graham's size, ten-year profitability and EPS growth tests, but it only started paying a dividend in 2024. Its trailing P/E of 17.8 and P/B of 7.0 multiply to about 123, far above his 22.5 limit.
summaries.thiel: Alphabet is close to Thiel's ideal of a monopoly: Google Search holds about 90% of global searches and was built from a big share of a small early market. Its proprietary technology (TPUs, Gemini, search ranking) and distribution are strong, but AI chatbots challenge whether that position is durable.
summaries.gerstner: Alphabet is one of the main beneficiaries of the AI platform shift Gerstner focuses on, with Google Cloud revenue up about 80% to $24.8B in Q2 2026 and its own TPU chips. Its forward P/E near 26 for revenue growth expected around 24% in 2026 looks reasonable on his growth-adjusted lens, though he has urged big tech to keep capex and costs disciplined.
summaries.druckenmiller: Alphabet fits Druckenmiller's focus on accelerating fundamentals and price confirmation: revenue growth is speeding up toward a consensus 24% in 2026 and the stock is up nearly 50% in a year. He would watch the risk that AI capex and antitrust remedies weigh on margins.
summaries.smith: Alphabet meets Smith's quality tests (ROIC about 25%, gross margin about 61%, little debt), but heavy AI capex has cut its free-cash-flow yield to about 1.2%. Smith has also been wary of dual-class governance and very high capex in technology companies.
summaries.greenblatt: Alphabet has a good return on capital (ROIC about 25%), but its EV/EBIT of 28.5 gives an earnings yield of only about 3.5%. It would rank only moderately on the Magic Formula today.
summaries.akre: Alphabet fits Akre's stool reasonably well: an extraordinary business, capable management and big reinvestment opportunities in Cloud, AI and Waymo. The open question is whether its $175-185B 2026 capex will earn returns as high as search did.
summaries.pabrai: Alphabet at a forward P/E of about 26 and near record highs is not a Dhandho-style cheap, distressed bet. It would have fitted better during the 2023-2025 periods when investors feared AI would destroy search.
summaries.wood: Alphabet fits Wood's framework well: it is an AI leader (Gemini, TPUs, DeepMind), runs the leading robotaxi service (Waymo) and works on quantum computing and AI drug discovery (Isomorphic Labs). It combines several innovation platforms, though its core ad business is mature.
summaries.ackman: Alphabet fits Ackman's criteria of a simple, dominant, cash-generative business with high barriers to entry; Pershing Square itself bought Alphabet shares in 2023. The weaker fits are antitrust exposure and capex-driven pressure on free cash flow.
summaries.sleep: Alphabet gives most of its consumer services (Search, Maps, Gmail, YouTube) away free, funded by ads, and its scale lets it run AI at low cost per query, which resembles Sleep's 'scale economics shared'. It does not cut prices to advertisers, so the fit is partial.
summaries.valentine: Google itself was a Sequoia investment (1999) and fits Valentine's focus on huge markets and technology that solves a big problem. Today it is a giant incumbent rather than an early-stage company, though Waymo and Cloud have that market-creating character.

momentum.evidence: GOOGL closed at $353.78 on 13 October 2026, up 49.6% over 52 weeks, versus a 17.3% price gain for the S&P 500 over the same period.

g4.evidence: Alphabet is led by Sundar Pichai with founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin still in control and Brin working on Gemini, and it was backed early by Sequoia and Kleiner Perkins.

g6.evidence: Some commentators question its AI capex and search risk, but most of the 62 covering analysts rate it Strong Buy with an average target of $430.40, well above the price.

simple.evidence: Its core business, selling ads alongside Google Search and YouTube plus renting cloud computing, is easy for a careful generalist to understand.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose every year from $182.5B in 2020 to $402.8B in 2025, and it has been profitable throughout.

integrity.evidence: Reporting is clear and it now pays a dividend and buys back stock, but dual-class shares give the founders voting control, and antitrust rulings found it illegally maintained its search monopoly.

b6.evidence: It mostly builds its own products, but it has a history of costly moonshots in Other Bets and has been accused of following rivals in areas such as short video and chatbots.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 25% and debt/equity is 0.19, with $242B of cash and marketable securities against $98B of debt in June 2026 (StockAnalysis, company filings).

fcf.evidence: Trailing free cash flow fell to $53.3B to June 2026, well under half of net income even excluding a $99B equity gain, because AI capex has surged.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings built YouTube, Android, Google Cloud and its AI stack, and market value has grown to about $4.3 trillion, far more than the earnings retained.

safety.evidence: At a forward P/E of about 26 and a free-cash-flow yield of 1.2%, the price is not well below a conservative estimate of value.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of 26.3 with consensus revenue growth of about 24% in 2026 is reasonable for its quality, but its PEG of about 1.9 is not cheap.

mu5.evidence: Its balance sheet and many businesses make failure unlikely, but AI chatbots, antitrust remedies on default deals and the ad-tech case are real ways its core search profits could shrink.

reinvest.evidence: It is reinvesting heavily ($175-185B capex planned for 2026) in Cloud and AI at a current ROIC of about 25%, but the returns on this new spending are not yet proven.

ly2.evidence: Alphabet is a fast-growing stalwart: a giant whose story is search and YouTube ads plus rapidly growing Cloud and AI.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of 17.8 is below recent EPS growth (from $8.04 in 2024 to $10.80 in 2025, +34%), but that P/E is flattered by investment gains and the forward PEG is about 1.9.

runway.evidence: Google Cloud revenue grew about 80% in Q2 2026, Gemini reached 950 million monthly users and Waymo is expanding, giving many years of growth potential.

ly7.evidence: The share count fell about 0.6% over the past year through buybacks, but insiders, mainly the founders who own about 9.9%, have been selling rather than buying.

ly8.evidence: Alphabet is one of the most widely owned and followed stocks, covered by 62 analysts.

fi2.evidence: As search matured it built YouTube, Android, Google Cloud, Gemini, TPUs and Waymo.

fi3.evidence: R&D produced the Transformer (2017), TPU chips, Gemini models and AlphaFold (2024 Nobel Prize), which now drive Cloud and AI products.

fi4.evidence: Its self-serve ad auction serves millions of advertisers, and default placement on Android, Chrome and Apple devices gives it unmatched reach to users.

longterm.evidence: It has funded long-term bets such as TPUs (from 2015), Waymo (since 2009) and quantum computing for years before they paid off.

gr1.evidence: Alphabet had $402.8B of 2025 revenue and a market capitalization of about $4.3 trillion.

ni10.evidence: Alphabet has been profitable every year for well over ten years, with net income of $132.2B in 2025.

gr4.evidence: Alphabet paid its first ever dividend in 2024, so it lacks a 20-year record.

eps10.evidence: EPS rose from $5.61 in 2021 to $10.80 in 2025, already nearly doubling in four years and far more over ten.

gr6.evidence: The trailing P/E is 17.8 (flattered by a $99B investment gain) and the forward P/E is 26.3, both above Graham's limit of about 15 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: P/E of 17.8 times P/B of 7.0 is about 123, far above Graham's 22.5 ceiling.

th1.evidence: Its search quality and TPU-based cost per AI query are leading, but rivals such as ChatGPT, Claude and NVIDIA GPUs are close substitutes rather than ten times worse.

timing.evidence: Its full AI stack (TPUs, DeepMind, Gemini) is paying off now, with Google Cloud revenue up about 80% to $24.8B in Q2 2026.

th3.evidence: Google started with a dominant share of the small late-1990s web search market and expanded into search advertising, video, mobile and cloud.

team.evidence: Sundar Pichai has led Alphabet since 2019, alongside DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis and CFO Anat Ashkenazi, with the founders still involved.

th5.evidence: It reaches billions of users through Android, Chrome and default search deals, and advertisers through its self-serve Google Ads platform.

durable.evidence: Search has held about 90% share for over 20 years, but AI answer engines and antitrust remedies make its position in 10-20 years less certain.

th7.evidence: PageRank and the auction ad model were unique insights in 1998-2002, but its current opportunities in AI and cloud are contested by well-funded rivals.

trend.evidence: Alphabet is a leading beneficiary of AI and cloud computing through Gemini, its own TPU chips and Google Cloud.

dr1.evidence: Revenue growth sped up from 13.9% in 2024 and 15.1% in 2025 to a consensus 23.9% for 2026, with Search up 17% and Cloud about 80% in Q2 2026.

dr2.evidence: Cloud backlog, TPU sales and Waymo growth could make it look better in two years, but antitrust and AI search risk cloud the picture.

dr4.evidence: Alphabet has net cash so rates matter little to its finances, but advertising revenue is sensitive to the economy.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include Q3 2026 results in late October 2026, Gemini model launches, external TPU sales and Waymo expansion.

dr7.evidence: Its momentum and quality support high conviction, but antitrust outcomes and AI capex returns argue against an outsized position.

gm.evidence: Trailing gross margin is 60.9%, high for a company running large data centres and a sign of pricing power in search ads.

fcfyield.evidence: The free-cash-flow yield is about 1.2% ($53.3B trailing FCF on a $4.3 trillion market cap), low because of heavy AI capex.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is 28.5, an earnings yield of about 3.5%, which is low by Magic Formula standards.

pa2.evidence: Alphabet is not in a setback now; fears that AI would destroy search have eased as revenue growth accelerated and the stock rose 49.6% in a year.

pa4.evidence: Its net cash and diverse businesses limit permanent loss, but structural risks to search profits from AI and antitrust are not small.

wo1.evidence: Alphabet is a leader in AI (Gemini, DeepMind, TPUs) and in autonomous driving through Waymo.

wo2.evidence: Its TPU chips and model efficiency cut the cost per AI query sharply as volume grows, though its ad prices are not falling.

wo3.evidence: It combines AI, autonomous vehicles (Waymo), cloud, quantum computing (Willow chip) and AI drug discovery (Isomorphic Labs).

wo4.evidence: Cloud, AI agents and robotaxis could greatly expand its market, but many-times growth in five years is uncertain for a $400B-revenue company.

ac3.evidence: It is insulated from commodity prices and rates, but advertising spending follows the economy and regulation is a major outside force.

ns1.evidence: Its scale funds free services for billions of users, but it does not pass savings back to advertisers through lower prices.

ns4.evidence: Cloud and AI should grow its position, but the future of search in an AI world makes it unclear it will be clearly stronger in 10-20 years.

va2.evidence: It solves the huge problem of finding information and reaching customers, for billions of users and millions of advertisers.
